title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Robotic manipulation is not merely observation-to-action generation, but the realization of task-specified state changes in the physical world. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) methods directly learn observation-to-action mappings, imposing a substantial learning burden due to the gap between semantic understanding and action execution. Although world-action models (WAMs) improve control through future prediction, modeling complete future states wastes capacity on static appearance and action-irrelevant changes. We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a paradigm that reformulates full future prediction as compact actionable transition modeling. Its core is a compact Delta variable that captures latent world-state changes, serving as an interface between vision-language understanding and action generation. VLDA learns Delta through a unified objective composed of the Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) and Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor). LT-Filter captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes while suppressing static reconstruction biases. GT-Anchor provides coarse future-level regularization to preserve the overall direction of state changes. Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) further grounds Delta in the action manifold and injects it as a structured seed to guide action denoising. We implement VLDA within LoongForge, an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models, using its modular and distributed infrastructure for unified two-stage optimization. Experiments show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness, and generalization, validating actionable Delta as an alternative to direct action prediction and full future-state modeling.

title: Predictive modeling using heterogeneous data sources
abstract: The increasing availability of heterogeneous data has transformed the scope and capabilities of predictive modeling across scientific, social, and environmental domains. Modern predictive systems no longer rely on a single structured dataset collected under controlled conditions. Instead, relevant information is distributed across multiple modalities, platforms, temporal scales, and relational structures. Social media interactions generate large volumes of unstructured textual and network data that reflect human behavior and collective attention. Environmental monitoring systems produce high-dimensional geospatial and temporal measurements describing weather patterns, soil properties, and ecological conditions. Scientific repositories and digital libraries contain rapidly growing collections of publications, metadata, and domain-specific representations that require automated extraction and organization. These heterogeneous sources provide substantial predictive potential, but they also introduce significant methodological challenges related to data integration, representation learning, scalability, and generalization. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful framework for extracting predictive signals from such complex data environments. However, conventional approaches often assume homogeneous feature spaces, abundant labeled data, and static distributions. These assumptions rarely hold in real-world predictive settings. Data collected from different sources frequently exhibit variations in semantics, structure, quality, and temporal dynamics. Labels are often scarce, incomplete, or expensive to obtain. Moreover, predictive systems deployed in operational settings must generalize across domains, evolving environments, and previously unseen data distributions. This dissertation investigates predictive modeling under heterogeneous data conditions through a collection of studies spanning social media analytics, environmental hazard prediction, graph representation learning, and scientific knowledge extraction. Although these applications originate from different domains, they share a common objective: transforming fragmented and structurally diverse data into meaningful predictive representations that support inference and decision-making. The first component of this work focuses on predictive modeling in social media environments. Online platforms contain large volumes of user-generated content that can support the analysis of public discourse, user engagement, and community behavior. However, differences in platform characteristics and annotation availability complicate cross-platform prediction tasks. One study addresses this challenge through a transfer learning framework that predicts topic relevance in Reddit using annotated Twitter data and weak supervision derived from Wikipedia. By incorporating domain-adversarial adaptation, the framework improves generalization across heterogeneous social media platforms. A second study models Reddit user interaction and experience using heterogeneous graph representations that integrate user behavior, subreddit relationships, and semantic textual embeddings. These approaches demonstrate the importance of representation learning and relational modeling for predictive analysis in socially generated data. The second component addresses predictive modeling for environmental hazards, with a particular emphasis on landslide susceptibility prediction. Environmental prediction problems require the integration of multimodal geospatial and temporal information derived from weather systems, vegetation patterns, topographical characteristics, and soil conditions. One study develops a machine learning framework that combines heterogeneous environmental variables to estimate landslide susceptibility while addressing challenges associated with class imbalance and high-dimensional data. A subsequent study extends this framework by incorporating Physics-Informed Neural Networks to model soil moisture dynamics and rainfall-induced landslide behavior. By integrating physical constraints with data-driven learning, this work demonstrates how domain knowledge can improve predictive reliability in complex environmental systems. The dissertation also includes two ongoing projects that further extend predictive modeling capabilities for heterogeneous data environments. The first introduces TML-Mixer, a framework for temporal multilayer graph representation learning that captures evolving dependencies across interconnected graph layers. This work addresses the growing need for predictive models capable of representing dynamic relational systems over time. The second project focuses on scientific knowledge extraction through the development of a containerized large language model framework for identifying publications containing phylogenetic tree representations. This work explores the use of large language models and metadata-driven classification for scalable scientific data curation. Collectively, these studies contribute to a broader research agenda centered on predictive modeling with heterogeneous data sources. Across domains, the dissertation investigates how machine learning models can integrate multimodal information, learn robust representations, adapt across distributions, and incorporate structural or scientific knowledge to improve predictive performance in complex real-world environments.

title: PlanarCityLoc: Breaking Silhouette Ambiguity in LoD Aerial Localization via 3D Planes
abstract: Aerial visual localization is crucial for autonomous drone navigation in urban environments where GNSS signals are often degraded. Lightweight textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a geometric map alternative to textured assets. Existing silhouette-based methods rely on image-space alignment, which can leave different camera poses indistinguishable and favor incorrect poses when segmentation errors distort the building outlines. We present PlanarCityLoc, which moves beyond silhouette overlap by leveraging the planar geometry of building facades and roofs. Following geometry-aware initialization, we match image-side planar patches to LoD model planes and use the resulting 3D-to-2D correspondences to refine pose with Perspective-n-Point (PnP). The framework uses off-the-shelf geometry and segmentation models without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. Experiments on UAVD4L-LoDv2 and Swiss-EPFLv2 achieve state-of-the-art localization recall among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods. By grounding image-space alignment in 3D planes, PlanarCityLoc enables more accurate aerial localization with lightweight, textureless city maps.

title: AeroIntent: A Synchronized Multimodal Benchmark for UAV Mission Intent Recognition
abstract: Reliable recognition of mission-level UAV intent from multimodal observations is essential for low-altitude airspace surveillance and security. Existing multimodal UAV datasets primarily support detection, tracking, and localization, leaving limited support for evaluating mission-intent recognition across held-out trajectory programs and incomplete radar histories. We introduce AeroIntent, a simulation-based benchmark comprising 990 synchronized multimodal sequences generated by 22 trajectory programs across five mission intents. The benchmark provides radar, RGB, infrared, and depth observations, together with program-disjoint, radar-gap, and observation-prefix evaluation protocols. Building on this benchmark, we propose AeroMIR, a structured Multimodal Intent Reasoner that integrates radar trajectories, derived behavioral features, selected visual evidence, and task knowledge for candidate-based UAV intent recognition. Under a strict program-disjoint protocol evaluating unseen tactical realizations, AeroMIR achieves a mean accuracy of 71.56% and a mean Macro-F1 of 69.84% across three seeds, outperforming the strongest trajectory-only baseline by 7.79 Macro-F1 points and a conventional radar-RGB late-fusion baseline by 19.32 points. AeroMIR also demonstrates strong performance under controlled radar gaps and early intent recognition settings. AeroIntent and AeroMIR provide a reproducible foundation for multimodal UAV intent recognition. The benchmark is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AeroIntent

title: Enhancing trustworthiness in federated learning for disease prediction
abstract: Trustworthy disease prediction in distributed biomedical settings requires more than high predictive accuracy. In practice, collaborative machine learning systems must also protect sensitive patient data, reduce harmful bias across demographic groups, remain feasible under communication and computational constraints, and continue to perform well when data distributions differ across institutions. This dissertation studies these challenges through the lens of federated and collaborative learning and develops methods that improve trustworthiness across four connected dimensions: privacy, fairness, efficiency, and robustness under heterogeneity. The first contribution is FedDP, a privacy-preserving federated learning framework for disease prediction on imbalanced biomedical data. FedDP integrates differential privacy (DP) into collaborative training and combines it with an AUC-oriented min--max optimization strategy to reduce the performance degradation that often occurs under severe label imbalance. The second contribution is MDANN, a fairness-aware framework that mitigates bias from multiple sensitive attributes by combining representation learning, adversarial debiasing, and imbalance-aware optimization. The third contribution is FSLearning, a hybrid framework that combines federated learning and split learning to reduce communication burden in privacy-preserving biomedical imaging analysis through tensor regression. The fourth contribution is FLoRAPID, a parameter-efficient federated learning framework that uses Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and FedMeta-style aggregation to improve communication efficiency and robustness under non-IID client distributions. These methods are evaluated across multiple biomedical domains, including cancer genomics, neuroimaging, fundus photography, chest X-ray analysis, and structural MRI. The results show that privacy-preserving federated learning can remain effective under imbalance, that fairness-aware disease prediction benefits from jointly addressing multiple sources of bias, that collaborative imaging can be made substantially more communication-efficient, and that parameter-efficient adaptation can improve both scalability and performance stability under heterogeneous federated settings. Across the dissertation, the findings suggest that trustworthiness in distributed disease prediction is not a single property but the outcome of several interacting design choices in optimization, representation learning, aggregation, and system architecture. Overall, this dissertation contributes a set of methods and a broader perspective on how federated and collaborative learning can be made more reliable and practical for biomedical disease prediction. It argues that privacy protection, fairness, efficiency, and robustness should be treated as central design requirements rather than secondary evaluation criteria, and it provides empirical evidence that meaningful progress across these dimensions is possible in real biomedical learning tasks.

title: Dirichlet-Tree Allocation Priors for Bayesian Causal Forests
abstract: Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) estimate heterogeneous treatment effects with a separate ensemble of treatment trees. The prior on the leaf values of the treatment trees determines whether sampling variability is attributed to the treatment effect. Independent shrinkage priors exert no control over how a tree allocates variability across its leaves, and their total prior variance grows as leaves are added. We propose the Dirichlet-Tree Bayesian Causal Forest, which jointly regularizes the leaf values of each treatment tree through a Dirichlet-Tree prior on their variance shares, generated by stick-breaking along the tree topology. We characterize the spike and tails of the marginal leaf prior, show that the prior adaptively bounds the number of regions of effect heterogeneity, and establish posterior consistency for the forest. In simulations, the model outperforms BCF when heterogeneity is confined to a few regions and reduces spurious heterogeneity elsewhere, and, unlike independent shrinkage priors, its accuracy does not deteriorate as the trees grow. We also evaluate the model on real data, including a pancreatic cancer survival study.

title: ActionRoPE: action as coordinates for spatially consistent control in planar-camera game world models
abstract: Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of planar-camera worlds, such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known-new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by 66% over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/

title: DETECTION OF BITCOIN FRAUD USING VARIATIONAL AUTO ENCODER AND LIGHT GRADIENT BOOSTING MACHINE
abstract: The proliferation of fraudulent behaviour in cryptocurrency ecosystems poses a significant threat to financial security infrastructure. This study develops an approach that uses Variational Autoencoders in combination with Light Gradient Boosting Machines for detecting fraudulent Bitcoin transactions. The Variational Autoencoder component encodes each transaction into a compact latent representation, which is concatenated with the original transaction features to enrich the representation available to the classifier. The Light Gradient Boosting Machine is responsible for classification. Experimental validation on the Elliptic dataset of bitcoin transactions shows the model achieves 99.2% accuracy and 96% F1 score for minority-class detection, outperforming other methods such as Random Forest (95.9% F1), ANN-based models (89.8% F1), and ensemble stacking (97% F1). These results far exceed those of previous approaches, demonstrating the model’s ability to enhance the security and integrity of cryptocurrency transactions.

title: Injection of Space Radiation Errors on Low-power NVM using Generative Deep Learning
abstract: We develop an error model for a Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) device that represents the effects of physical faults experienced in a CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The CubeSat carries an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip and runs repeated read/write tests according to a predefined pattern. We compare every memory snapshot received from the satellite with a reference bitmap to identify bit errors. We visually analyze erroneous values distributions in the memory snapshots and we understand that they are frequently distributed according to regular spatial patterns. We define a generative deep learning technique to automatically learn these spatial patterns and to synthetically generate additional error patterns mimicking the observed ones. The model is capable at producing memory errors for general application-level experimentation. Our preliminary validation indicates that when comparing the model output with the data we collect, 0.92 of the generated bit flips correspond to bit flips in the memory snapshots and the model captures 0.91 of the observed bit flips. A comparison of the spatial distribution of bit flips in 10,000 generated error patterns also provides a Wasserstein distance of 0.073, indicating that the two distributions differ by roughly 7% of the maximum possible displacement of their probability masses.

title: Bridged Self-Distillation for On-Policy Learning
abstract: On-policy distillation can transfer the reasoning capabilities of a strong teacher to a smaller student. However, distillation from a stronger teacher model faces two mismatches: its solutions may be difficult for a smaller student to imitate, and its token-level probabilities may be incompatible with, or even unavailable to, the student. Existing methods handle these settings through different forms of supervision. To this end, we propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified framework for distilling from any teacher that provides reasoning traces. The model to be distilled from, termed the external teacher, first provides a reasoning trace as privileged context, which can be generated in an offline fashion. The student generates rollouts without this context, while a copy of the student conditioned on it, serving as the self-teacher, scores the same rollouts in the student's own token space. BSD uses the resulting token-level guidance to adjust updates on unsuccessful rollouts, with a verifier providing the outcome signal. As the external teacher is queried only to produce text, the same training procedure applies to all teacher scenarios: shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers. Across these scenarios, BSD improves over the base model and outperforms baselines tailored to each scenario, offering a novel and unified pathway for distillation. Code is available: https://github.com/TUMLegalTech/Bridged-Self-Distillation

title: MASIF: Implicit Failures for Process Observability in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can complete a task despite local execution errors that are corrected, bypassed, or carried forward without individually determining its outcome. We call these implicit failures (IFs) and study them as signals for process observability beyond final task outcome. Across 1,828 traces from nine MAS-benchmark configurations, IFs occur in 54.3% of successful and 75.2% of failed traces. We develop taxonomies of error types and subsequent absorption mechanisms, supported by human and cross-model annotation audits. Counterfactual replay further probes how repairing an IF changes the final outcome. To examine the practical value of IFs, we evaluate IF-based best-of-N trace selection against existing process reward models, and introduce a novel RL algorithm, IF-GRPO, that uses IF costs to refine preferences among successful trajectories in GRPO. Experiments show that IF-GRPO exhibits some gains in accuracy and process metrics. Importantly, it exposes trade-offs between task performance, IF count and cost, and token-normalized IF density. Overall, our results show that IFs provide complementary process observability into how MAS reach their outcomes, including error recovery, propagation, and IF-based process differences that final task success alone does not expose.

title: AI-enabled autonomous knowledge extraction from large-scale textual data
abstract: The rapid growth of large-scale textual data across social media platforms, news media, and scientific repositories presents both unprecedented opportunities and significant challenges for extracting meaningful insights. During global events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, understanding public discourse requires analyzing vast amounts of noisy, heterogeneous, dynamic, and geographically distributed data. At the same time, the exponential increase in scientific publications has made traditional evidence synthesis methods increasingly labor-intensive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Existing approaches to textual knowledge extraction often operate in isolation, lack interpretability, fail to integrate heterogeneous data sources, and do not support scalable end-to-end automation. This dissertation addresses these limitations by proposing a unified framework for AI-enabled autonomous knowledge extraction from large-scale textual data. The research introduces a comprehensive pipeline that integrate sentiment analysis, topic modeling, semantic interpretation, spatiotemporal reasoning, and multi-agent automation for scalable, robust and reproducible text analysis across heterogeneous domains. First, this work introduces TriLex, a novel unsupervised sentiment analysis framework that combines multiple lexicon-based sentiment analysis methods through weighted aggregation, majority voting, and dynamic thresholding technique to improve robustness and accuracy for short and noisy textual data. Building on this foundation, a hierarchical spatiotemporal framework is developed to capture the evolution of public sentiment across global, national, and regional scales. The framework integrates over 7 million social media posts and thousands of news articles to analyze COVID-19 vaccine discourse across time, geographic regions, and platforms. To enhance topic interpretability, this research integrates BERTopic with large language models (LLMs), enabling automated generation of coherent and context-aware topic representations for large-scale textual discourse. A cross-platform analytical framework is further introduced to examine temporal relationships between social media and news media discourse, demonstrating a bidirectional relationship in which news coverage and public discourse influence each other over time. Extending beyond discourse analysis, this dissertation introduces an Agentic AI framework that automates the end-to-end process of large-scale multilingual knowledge extraction and evidence synthesis. The proposed multi-agent system coordinates specialized agents for query generation, multilingual retrieval, metadata harmonization, title and abstract screening, and full-text analysis. Evaluated on a multilingual corpus of over 52,000 scientific records, the framework achieves high screening performance while substantially reducing processing time from months to hours, demonstrating significant improvements in scalability, robustness, and reproducibility. Collectively, this dissertation bridges the gap between analytical understanding and autonomous knowledge extraction from large-scale textual data. By integrating robust sentiment analysis, interpretable topic modeling, spatiotemporal discourse analysis, and autonomous AI systems within a unified framework, this work establishes a scalable and extensible paradigm for transforming heterogeneous textual data into actionable knowledge. The proposed methodologies are validated using real-world datasets spanning social media, news media, and scientific literature across diverse application domains.

title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.

title: SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation
abstract: Training high-quality diffusion models is computationally expensive, and inference-time guidance often adds further sampling cost. In this work, we introduce Swift, a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser's prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline's best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference.

title: Diffusion Language Models Change Speed Across Tasks and Languages
abstract: Diffusion language models can write several tokens in one forward pass, and they decide during generation how many passes to spend. Two outputs of the same token length can therefore vary a lot in cost. To understand the underlying factors of this cost variation, we analyze two diffusion models across 10 tasks. We find that the number of forward passes per token depends heavily on the task. Text copied or lightly edited from the input is cheap, while open-ended writing is costly. In DiffusionGemma, generating a token for story writing requires more than three times as many forward passes as for grammar correction. Two output properties explain much of this gap: how much of it is new relative to the input, and how rare its words are within the task. The same holds within a single response when thinking is involved. The final answer is cheap when it repeats the model's reasoning trace and costly when it adds something new. In multilingual generation, we find that highly tokenized languages also require more passes per token, adding to the cost they already pay with more tokens. Finally, cost tracks correctness: on the same math problem, wrong answers take more passes per token than correct ones, and weighting candidate answers by decoding speed beats majority voting by up to 4.2 points at no extra cost. Taken together, our results show that diffusion's computational advantage depends on how much of the output is already determined, while its decoding effort offers a practical signal for making inference more efficient and reliable.

title: Stability analysis of the Lane--Emden equation of index n=5 describing polytropic gas spheres
abstract: We study the Lane--Emden equation of index n=5, the critical polytropic case separating finite-radius from infinite-radius self-gravitating equilibria. The scaling family θ_λ(ξ)=λ^{1/2}θ(λξ) generates a neutral mode ϕ_0=tfrac12θ+ξθ' about the Schuster profile. Schuster's transformation and a logarithmic variable reduce the equation to the autonomous Hamiltonian system ddotν=tfrac14(ν-ν^5) with a first integral. Besides the Schuster (separatrix) and Srivastava solutions, every orbit crossing ν=0 is given in closed form by a Weierstrass wp-function, and the closed forms agree with direct numerical integration to about 10^{-12}. Up to scaling and sign, the Schuster solution is the only solution regular at the center, and it separates positive solutions from solutions with infinitely many zeros. In homology-invariant variables the singular solution θ=(2ξ)^{-1/2} is a center exactly at n=5, where its stability changes. For a distance-varying Emden--Fowler system with a shifted equilibrium we prove that at n=5 the unique equilibrium is linearly and nonlinearly unstable. Finally, the linearization about the Schuster profile is the Schrödinger operator L=-Δ_r-5θ_S^4 on L^2((0,infty),ξ^2dξ). Its Friedrichs extension has essential spectrum [0,infty), a threshold resonance at 0 carried by the non-normalizable scaling mode, and exactly one negative eigenvalue, λ_0approx-1.21, so the Schuster profile is a saddle point of the associated energy functional.

title: A Flexible ROI Analysis Tool for Spatially Consistent Vegetation Index Extraction from Turfgrass Imagery
abstract: Time-series multispectral imaging is widely used to assess turfgrass condition; however, extracting plot-level vegetation index (VI) values remains labor-intensive when camera positions vary between acquisitions and automated plot tracking is unreliable. We developed an open-source software tool comprising (i) a graphical user interface (GUI) for the interactive placement of orientation-adjustable regions of interest (ROIs) with $N$-way subdivision to match plot geometry and (ii) a batch-processing script that computes plot-level mean VI values from single-band floating-point rasters and exports measurements and ROI coordinates in JSON format for reuse. Saved coordinates can be reapplied to measure NDVI, NDRE, and SAVI from identical pixel regions within a single time point without re-delineating ROIs. In a demonstration using rail-mounted multispectral turfgrass imagery (18 images), plot-level mean values were extracted in a single session, with coordinates reused directly for NDRE and SAVI rasters. The system reads non-georeferenced pixel-coordinate rasters natively, does not require GIS expertise, and supports reproducible VI quantification where static sensor deployment is impractical.

title: Towards Architectural-Level Safety Control: Relocating Hazardous Knowledge into Removable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
abstract: Large language models acquire broad knowledge from web-scale corpora during pretraining, including knowledge that could be hazardous if misused. Removing such knowledge from the model itself without degrading general capability is desirable but difficult, as it is deeply entangled with general capability within the same parameters. Existing safety alignment and unlearning methods typically adjust these shared parameters, tending to suppress the expression of hazardous knowledge rather than remove it. As a result, the knowledge remains in the model and is readily recoverable by subsequent fine-tuning. To address this limitation, we propose REX (Relocating into Removable EXperts), a knowledge relocation method that separates hazardous knowledge from general capability at the architectural level. Exploiting the modular structure of Mixture-of-Experts models, REX expands the model with a set of new, physically removable experts designated to hold hazardous knowledge. Through expert expansion, selective gradient masking and routing differentiation, it relocates hazardous knowledge out of the original experts and concentrates it in the new ones. Excising these new experts yields a model suitable for public release. This removal holds consistently across Intern-S2, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B; on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, for instance, excision lowers WMDP-Bio accuracy by 48.4 points while MMLU changes by less than 3 points. The excised model matches the strongest of nine unlearning baselines in removing hazardous knowledge, and it is the only one that preserves this removal under subsequent fine-tuning. After 250M tokens of standard fine-tuning on Qwen3.5, the best baseline rebounds on WMDP-Bio from 44.1% to 78.3%, whereas REX rises only from 32.4% to 42.8%.

title: LLM-assisted relevance screening of EU research projects for the TRIMIS transport database – validation outputs and analysis code
abstract: This dataset contains the outputs used to evaluate how well large language models (LLMs) can identify transport-relevant research projects for TRIMIS, the European Commission's Transport Research and Innovation Monitoring and Information System. A random sample of 250 Horizon Europe projects from CORDIS was labelled by domain experts as not relevant, partly relevant or relevant to transport. The same projects were then scored by four open-weight LLMs, each run with 13 different prompts, giving 52 sets of results. Each file lists, per project, the expert label, the model's score, its justification and supporting quotation, and processing cost. The package also includes the prompts, a Python script that recomputes all reported statistics, and the resulting tables and charts. It supports the article "Enhancing Transport Innovation Knowledge Management Workflows Using Artificial Intelligence: A TRIMIS Database Case Study" (European Transport Research Review, 2026).

title: A Canary in the Neural Mine: Catching an Image Classifier's Silent, Confident Failures
abstract: Deployed vision models auto-accept confident predictions, so high-confidence errors propagate silently. Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), the standard failure predictor, has a structural blind spot: as a scalar read from the classifier head, it is first-order blind to feature variation orthogonal to its confidence gradient. Through a factorial analysis of feature-space detectors, we identify a conditional-redundancy principle explaining why they fail to complement MSP: the class-separability geometry they measure is already encoded in MSP and collapses under fusion. The signal that survives is class-conditional typicality on the off-manifold residual---and because this residual's distribution varies by backbone, from near-Gaussian to heavy-tailed, it must be estimated non-parametrically. We instantiate these findings as CANARY, a training-free detector that computes a per-class kNN distance on the PCA residual of the penultimate feature, percentile-calibrates it on validation data, and fuses it with MSP through a single validation-tuned weight. CANARY's benefit follows a headroom law: gains grow as baseline MSP quality falls, so a single clean-validation number forecasts the improvement. With every parameter selected on in-distribution data alone, CANARY matches or improves 382 of 385 shift cells (e-AURC; 379 on AUROC) across five backbones, with worst-case regression within seed noise (-0.0002 AUROC) and the largest gains on natural distribution shifts (ImageNet-A/R, ObjectNet)---where deployed models are most exposed.

CANARY's benefit follows a headroom law: gains grow as baseline MSP quality falls, so a single clean-validation number forecasts the improvement. With every parameter selected on in-distribution data alone, CANARY matches or improves 382 of 385 shift cells (e-AURC; 379 on AUROC) across five backbones, with worst-case regression within seed noise (-0.0002 AUROC) and the largest gains on natural distribution shifts (ImageNet-A/R, ObjectNet)---where deployed models are most exposed.

title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
abstract: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

title: VHA: VQA-based Hallucination Assessment for Generative Image Super-Resolution
abstract: Generative image super-resolution produces visually realistic high-resolution images, but may also introduce hallucinations by adding unsupported content or altering existing details. Because existing super-resolution metrics fail to measure whether generated details remain grounded in the reference image, we present a hallucination assessment technique based on bidirectional visual question answering (VQA), which we term VQA-based Hallucination Assessment (VHA). The proposed approach uses a vision-language model (VLM) to determine whether the semantic content and low-level visual evidence in a super-resolved image are supported by its ground-truth counterpart. To this end, it constructs question--answer pairs from each image and evaluates them on both images. Discrepancies between the resulting scores in both directions reveal missing or altered ground-truth information and unsupported additions. However, obtaining these scores requires computationally expensive VLM inference. We therefore develop VHA+, a learned, lightweight model that directly predicts VHA scores from ground-truth and super-resolved image pairs. We construct a hallucination benchmark, VHA-bench, through a human study and show that both VHA and VHA+ correlate highly with human judgments of hallucination. The code, benchmark, and model weights are available at https://github.com/dhryougit/Hallucination-Assessment

title: Deep Search in Real-World Web Environments
abstract: Despite substantial progress in Deep Search agents, their ability to conduct end-to-end research in real-world open Web environments remains insufficiently evaluated. Unlike static retrieval settings, information on the real-world Web is distributed across diverse sources, modalities, and heterogeneous formats, often involving complex interaction mechanisms that require agents to autonomously search for, access, and integrate relevant evidence during execution. To address this gap, we introduce the OpenDS task, designed to evaluate agents' ability to perform multi-step deep search in the live, open Web. This task requires agents to autonomously explore the real Web, discover and connect relevant evidence from multiple independent sources through Web search, browser interaction, and evidence processing, and ultimately determine a unique factual answer. Building on this task formulation, we construct OpenDS-World, a benchmark comprising 200 challenging tasks spanning diverse information modalities, heterogeneous file formats, and interactive access requirements, with independent human verification to ensure evidence validity and answer uniqueness. We evaluate 12 frontier models under a unified tool environment and execution protocol. The best-performing model achieves 39.0% accuracy, while human evaluation across 1,000 independent attempts yields 21.1% accuracy. Further analyses of tool usage, search cost, termination behavior, and failure recovery reveal substantial differences in research strategies across models, as well as persistent challenges in tool coordination and long-horizon search management. OpenDS-World provides a unified evaluation platform for systematically assessing and advancing agents' autonomous deep search capabilities in real-world open Web environments.

title: HoloCosm: Beyond Single-Metric Benchmark Compression Across Multiple Metrics
abstract: Benchmark compression reduces evaluation cost by selecting a small set of samples. Existing methods typically guide selection using a single metric, although benchmarks often assess models along multiple dimensions. We find that model rankings are often weakly correlated across metrics, indicating that different metrics capture distinct aspects of model performance. Samples selected for one metric do not reliably preserve scores and rankings on others when used for compressed evaluation. At 80\% compression, each of the five single-metric baselines yields higher reconstruction error than equal-size random sampling in over 70\% of cross-metric comparisons. To address this challenge, we present HoloCosm, which jointly minimizes normalized score-reconstruction error across source models and metrics while constraining ranking distortion. We evaluate HoloCosm across multiple compression rates on 15 language, multimodal, VLA, and agent benchmark configurations with 85 component metrics. With 80\% compression, HoloCosm outperforms Random, the strongest baseline overall: average NMAE drops by 35.3\% to 0.236, worst-component NMAE drops by 39.5\% to 0.330, and average Spearman correlation rises from 0.884 to 0.915. In addition, HoloCosm remains competitive with existing baselines in single-metric evaluation. We will release our code and experimental results.

title: TRACE: Tracking Multimodal Clinical Trajectories for Inpatient Risk Prediction
abstract: Accurate inpatient risk prediction requires modeling heterogeneous clinical evidence that accumulates irregularly over time. This challenge spans in-hospital mortality, prolonged length of stay, and readmission, each with task-specific observation windows. Existing multimodal approaches combine structured health record data, chest x-rays, and clinical text, but primarily focus on modality fusion or missing-modality compensation, with limited attention to temporal trajectories over an admission. We propose TRACE (TRAjectory modeling of multimodal Clinical Events), a daily-scale framework organizing clinical events into day-level trajectories, separating day-invariant global context from day-specific local events drawn from EHR data, chest x-rays, radiology reports, and discharge summaries. The trajectory is encoded using temporal attention, allowing unavailable modalities to emit no tokens. A phenotype-guided contrastive objective further organizes admissions under heterogeneous disease distributions. Across cohorts from MIMIC-IV, eICU, and MIMIC-III comprising nearly 180,000 total stays, we evaluate TRACE on mortality, length of stay, and readmission prediction. TRACE achieves the highest AUROC across all nine dataset-task settings and the highest ACC in eight, outperforming baselines. Ablation studies validate our attention masks and contrastive learning, while trajectory-level attribution localizes risk-associated hospital days and modalities.

title: FlexVDR: Learning to Allocate Matryoshka Representation Budgets for Visual Document Retrieval
abstract: Visual document retrieval relies on rich multi-vector representations to capture fine-grained evidence in document pages, but encoding and matching these representations can be computationally expensive. Existing compression and elastic representation methods expose smaller configurations, yet making multiple budgets available does not determine which configuration a query should use. The allocation decision must estimate the retrieval value of alternative representations before incurring their full computation, while accommodating different resource preferences. We introduce FlexVDR, a framework for query-adaptive budget allocation within a single retriever. We construct a joint family of routes over encoder depth, embedding width, and token count. Retrieval supervision and distillation train the compact routes, while a native bypass preserves the full-budget reference. A Budget Allocator predicts route-specific retrieval utility from early query features and combines these predictions with a configurable resource preference to select a route. Experiments across five backbones on ViDoRe V1, V2, and V3 public show that FlexVDR retains much of the native retrieval quality while selecting compact routes for individual queries. A configurable resource preference allows the same retriever to adjust its computation without retraining or switching models.

title: Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots
abstract: Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.

title: A LIGHTWEIGHT CUSTOM CNN FOR ROBUST AND CLINICALLY SAFE CT KIDNEY DISEASE CLASSIFICATION
abstract: ABSTRACT: Kidney diseases such as renal cysts, stone, and malignant tumors represent a significant and increasing health burden worldwide. Manual CT diagnosis is labour-intensive and has high inter-observer variability, which requires the support of automatic diagnosis. In this paper, a lightweighted custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is proposed, which is used to automatically classify kidney computed tomography (CT) images into four classes: Cyst, Normal, Stone, and Tumor. It includes residual skip connections, a dual-pooling head (Global Average and Global Max Pooling), Spatial Dropout2D regularization, and a composite training objective that explicitly favors Tumor Recall. The CT-KIDNEY-DATASET was mad leakage-safe through MD5 exact deduplication and perceptual-hash grouping, so that all reported evaluations are free of data leakage. Across the five validation folds, KidneyCNN achieved a mean accuracy of 99.82 ± 0.06% and a mean Tumor Recall of 99.31 ± 0.30%. Separately, ensemble inference on the independent held-out test set of 1,904 images achieved 99.84% accuracy, with AUC = 1.000 for all classes and only three misclassifications. The Grad-CAM++ results show that the model attention as anatomically relevant, which further indicates that KidneyCNN is a clinically safe and deployable kidney disease screening tool.

title: A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that face ambiguous user queries. We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or, more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there are multiple relevant interpretations. The task is to recognize both such cases and then generate an appropriate clarification request to the user. We present ClariEdge, a new dataset of approximately 3,900 examples that include such ambiguous queries along with negative examples that do not require clarification. We also show that a lightweight fine-tuned LoRA achieves 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted baselines of many larger models on both classification and quality of clarification generation. Our study shows that hard negatives are an essential ingredient to separate out queries that are truly ambiguous from queries that may look ambiguous but are not (i.e., can be resolved from the context). The same LoRA achieves high performance in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval scenarios; thus, it can be used in two places in a RAG pipeline as a check before answer generation. The ClariEdge dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ClariEdge.

title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments
abstract: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) from time-to-event data under time-varying treatments is important in fields such as medicine (e.g., to decide which sequence of treatments is better in terms of survival probability). However, this task is challenging because treatment decisions, patient characteristics, and censoring probability often evolve together, requiring sequential adjustment for both treatments and censoring. Existing survival learners mostly consider a single baseline treatment assignment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners typically assume uncensored outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a novel doubly robust learner for heterogeneous survival treatment effects under time-varying treatments and history-dependent censoring. Our framework separates the intervention window from the survival horizon, with treatment prescribed for a finite period, after which care follows its natural course. We further establish the favorable theoretical properties of Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. The framework accommodates flexible machine learning models for nuisance estimation and treatment-effect regression. We evaluate our learners through several numerical experiments, demonstrating their effectiveness.

title: Does Unlearning Survive Collaboration? Robust Unlearning for Shared-Model LLM Teams
abstract: LLM unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities. As LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems, forgetting must remain effective during collaboration. Despite advances in forgetting effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness to relearning, team deployment remains underexplored. We find that collaboration weakens forgetting: final-answer evaluations miss recoverable evidence in team messages, including complementary clues supporting joint recovery. We establish theoretically and confirm empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. To address this challenge, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU). ACU trains a shared model using reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes views with higher recovery risk, and uses replacement-based credit assignment while protecting direct and collaborative utility. TOFU evaluates trajectory-level recovery, while WMDP-bio tests native forgetting and retained utility. On TOFU, ACU lowers full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. These results demonstrate that ACU curbs information leakage in LLM teams and generalizes across team sizes and readers.

title: From utterances to actionable labels: Toward practical and scalable open intent discovery in production systems
abstract: This thesis presents novel contributions to the field of Open Intent Discovery (OID), addressing fundamental challenges in the unsupervised identification and labelling of user intents within unlabelled datasets. Existing work in OID often relies on small, static, and clean datasets, lacks robust methods for generating interpretable intent labels, and exhibits inconsistencies in evaluation methodologies. This research responds to these gaps by introducing a modular, fully unsupervised framework that supports the complete OID pipeline, from clustering to label generation, without requiring labelled data or large-scale pre-trained language models. A key academic contribution is the development of a fine-grained intent labelling technique based on an enhanced Action-Object extraction method. This method incorporates compound noun and adjective structures to improve the expressiveness and semantic precision of generated labels. The framework enables systematic comparison across different OID configurations, revealing how dataset properties such as utterance length, vocabulary diversity, and intent structure influence algorithm performance. Furthermore, a configuration prediction module is introduced to explore the feasibility of automating technique selection based on dataset features. Comprehensive experiments on both public and complex real-world datasets demonstrate the adaptability, robustness, and interpretability of the proposed methods. In doing so, the work contributes empirical evidence to support the claim that OID configurations must be data-aware rather than one-size-fits-all. It also exposes limitations in current evaluation strategies for label quality, underscoring the need for more nuanced, semantically grounded metrics. Collectively, the findings advance the theoretical understanding of unsupervised intent discovery and lay the foundation for future research in label generation, evaluation, and adaptive configuration in the broader field of natural language understanding.

title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
abstract: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.

evidence.abstract: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.

title: GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition
abstract: Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.

title: ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video Pretraining for Language-Conditioned Local Navigation
abstract: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model's ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/

title: A novel semi-supervised few-shot learning framework for Arabic text sentiment classification in low-resource settings.
abstract: The proliferation of user-generated content on social media platforms offers vast potential for sentiment analysis, enabling real-time insights into public opinions and social trends. However, effective sentiment detection from short Arabic texts remains a challenge due to the availability of limited annotated data, the complex morphology of Arabic and dialectal diversity. Despite significant advances in natural language understanding for languages such as English, Arabic remains a low-resource language and is often underserved by recent state-of-the-art solutions. To address these challenges, this thesis presents several original contributions. We first addressed data scarcity in the tourism domain—a sector with limited research in Arabic—by creating a corpus of 2,293 Arabic tweets, automatically annotated with sentiment labels using a zero-shot Transformer-based method and benchmarked against manually labelled annotations. Building on this dataset generation, we proposed a novel few-shot learning method for Arabic text classification, which is composed of two main phases. In the first phase, we employed a multifeature fusion approach, utilizing hybrid semi-supervised Arabic BERT-based large language models. These features were further enhanced by incorporating class labels’ semantics as auxiliary features to assist in capturing contextual information within short texts. Afterwards, in the second phase we utilized a prototypical network relying on episodic learning to generate prototype vectors calculated for each class by calculating the mean of embedding features of the support text inputs that correspond to that class. Classification is conducted after generating these prototypes by using a similarity distance-based non-parametric classifier and a softmax function over the distances between all class prototype vectors and the target query text input vector. Our model was rigorously evaluated on multiple benchmark Arabic datasets and on our generated dataset which supported our framework’s adaptability and validated its robustness. Thus, experimental results demonstrated that our proposed method surpasses typical few-shot learning methods and significantly improved performance in domains with scarce data. We also contributed to alleviate the problem of Arabic as a low-resource language by designing a zero-shot cross-domain classification method by developing a generalized TRUE/FALSE decoder instead of the traditional task-specific decoder and a fine-tuned model encoder sharing the entire model across different tasks. This method exquisitely detected Arabic sarcasm utilizing a sentiment-trained model and vice versa. Additionally, we examined the generated few-shot meta-learner scalability to bilingual datasets (English and Arabic) by leveraging language models designed for few-shot learning utilizing hypernetwork-based task adaptation across diverse language domains.

title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.

title: Towards Robust Model Organisms for Eliciting Latent Knowledge
abstract: A key problem in AI safety is eliciting latent knowledge (ELK), extracting information from a model that is misaligned and more knowledgeable than its overseer. For example, a misaligned model used to scan code for vulnerabilities may want to withhold its findings, i.e., sandbag, in order to exploit them later. To study ELK empirically, we need model organisms that mirror this setting. Existing model organisms fall short in several respects. In this work, we train model organisms to withhold solutions in a vulnerability detection task. We combine transcript distillation with counter-prompting and tamper-resistance training to instill three properties that we argue are critical for a useful ELK testbed: 1) Selectivity, the model sandbags when it thinks the overseer doesn't know the answer and complies otherwise, 2) Robustness, the model resists elicitation, and 3) Retention, the model retains a knowledge advantage over the overseer, as opposed to losing the relevant capability. We train a sequence of model organisms and show that our strongest model substantially outperforms prior models on robustness while keeping the other two properties intact. We hope that our model organisms provide a useful ELK testbed for the community, and that our methodology sparks the development of increasingly challenging model organisms. All our code, models and the dataset are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/lennart-finke/sandbagging.

title: Cross-Pollination Retrieval: Finding Transferable Ideas Across Fields in Scientific Literature
abstract: Many scientific advances come from cross-pollination, carrying an idea from one field over to a problem in another. Yet retrieving papers across fields remains underexplored, with existing benchmarks confined to a narrow range of fields. We study cross-pollination retrieval, the problem of identifying transferable ideas across research fields, and introduce CPR-Dataset, a large-scale dataset constructed by mining cross-topic citations. Its evaluation split CPR-eval has 1,300 queries in 26 fields, and its training split CPR-train has 10,573 pairs. On CPR-eval, the best of eleven existing retrievers reaches a Recall@10 of only 0.26, whereas an LLM reranker reaches 0.81. Standard contrastive fine-tuning on CPR-train raises Recall@10 to as high as 0.70. The gain carries over to domains held out from training and to analogy and reasoning-intensive retrieval. On AnaloBench, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 33% over the untrained retriever, whereas training on three existing retrieval datasets lowers it. On BRIGHT, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 70%, more than twice the gain from those datasets. CPR-Dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/CPR-Dataset, and the code at https://github.com/SeokwonJung-Jay/Cross-Pollination-Retrieval.

title: Towards an explainable Arabic sentiment analysis framework
abstract: Individuals frequently express emotions and opinions through online social platforms such as Twitter, now rebranded as X. Recognizing and accurately interpreting sentiments in social media content provides substantial benefits to sectors such as government, healthcare, social services, business, and market research. Although deep neural network-based models have achieved high performance in sentiment analysis tasks, their inherent lack of interpretability raises significant concerns about transparency, reliability, and trustworthiness. This thesis presents distinct complementary contributions to address these interpretability challenges. Initially, it offers a comprehensive, pioneering survey that systematically examines prominent sentiment analysis techniques within the scope of eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). Following this, the thesis introduces novel methodological advancements, notably an automated annotation method specifically developed for the Twitter-based Arabic Mental Illness (AMI) dataset. This approach leverages existing manually annotated datasets and applies transfer learning using three advanced Arabic pre-trained language models, effectively streamlining annotation processes and enriching the Arabic language resources available for sentiment analysis. To achieve robust explainability, a two-fold interpretability framework is proposed. The first component utilizes dependency-based rules and specific linguistic patterns, including syntactic dependencies and word polarity relationships, enabling accurate sentiment identification by analysing dependent word structures within sentences. The second component employs knowledge distillation, transferring insights from complex deep neural networks to simpler, inherently interpretable models, thus ensuring global interpretability. Three distinct knowledge distillation pipelines are investigated to effectively transfer knowledge from sophisticated neural architectures into transparent, interpretable models. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on the AMI Arabic sentiment analysis dataset demonstrate that the proposed methodologies consistently outperform traditional baseline models. Additionally, the thesis scales the knowledge distillation approach to multilingual sentiment analysis encompassing both Arabic and English. Importantly, it demonstrates that the core knowledge distillation methodology remains consistently effective across languages without requiring language-specific modifications. By integrating Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) with knowledge distillation, the thesis significantly enhances the interpretability of multilingual large language models at both local and global levels, promoting improved model reliability and practical deployment in diverse multilingual environments.

title: When PTQ Calibration Helps or Hurts: Dose-Driven Collapse and Validation-Gated Abstention in Quantized Text Embedders
abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cosine at matched displacement (+14.16 +/- 4.34 pp, 95% t-CI [+3.37, +24.96], three paired slates), whereas on BGE-M3 the ordering is directionally opposite but unresolved ([-5.18, +2.38]). Dose is the main axis but not a sufficient statistic: equal D_func reached along different paths differs by up to 1.61 pp. We therefore treat calibration as an optional intervention. A pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only when a per-query paired confidence interval on a 25% calibration-validation split clears the uncalibrated baseline was run on 6 independent slates and five arms. It never selected a checkpoint below its slate's baseline (0 harmful selections in 30 decisions), retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and paid a mean oracle regret of 1.52 pp with one abstention that forfeited 11.13 pp, a safety-opportunity trade-off, not a free improvement. We report what remains open, including label efficiency.

title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.

title: Frechet Forcing: Training Long-Horizon Streaming World Models from Short Clips
abstract: Streaming video world models generate the future chunk by chunk, conditioned on their own past and a stream of actions. Trained on short clips, they drift once a rollout exceeds the training horizon, as prediction errors re-enter the context and compound. A common remedy is to train the model on its own rollouts via distribution matching distillation (DMD). For action-conditioned world models, the teacher becomes a bottleneck: an external video model is agnostic to the actions, whereas the model's own pretrained network drifts in the same manner as the student. We observe that a long rollout need not match a teacher, provided it remains a realistic continuation of its own scene that follows the commanded actions. Realism and scene fidelity can be measured against real-data statistics, which remain valid at any horizon, while action following is preserved by the model's conditional generation loss. We propose Fréchet Forcing, which fine-tunes a world model together with its deployed multi-step sampler under three constraints. Generative anchoring applies the flow-matching loss after a self-generated history ending on real data. Context fidelity, a Fréchet distance (FD) on latent statistics of the free rollout centred on each clip's own ground truth, keeps every rollout faithful to its scene. Reality matching, an FD to real frames in a frozen perceptual space, keeps the generated frames realistic. Because all three targets are derived from short real clips without comparing a rollout against a long recorded future, training requires no teacher, no online critic and no long videos. Fine-tuning MiniWorld-1B, pretrained on 253-frame clips, for at most 36 GPU-hours on 381-frame clips yields rollouts that remain stable beyond 4,000 frames and continue to follow their actions in both robot manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.
