title: Artificial Human: Genuine Need as a Precondition for Genuine AGI
abstract: We argue that a system with substantial processing capacity can be a genuine artificial general intelligence (AGI) — an independent agent rather than a computing system — only if its processing is coupled to a genuine need. We call a system that satisfies this condition an artificial human. Our claims are three. First, processing alone is not enough and need alone is not enough: genuine need must sit alongside processing (c = p·b; Rezaei, 2026a), and an AGI without genuine need is, on our view, a computing system and not an independent person. Second, the architecture must be two-loop, in the form of AIWBN (Rezaei, 2026b): the processing loop must not be able to access, suppress, or route around the need loop, and if the need is neutralized by any fixed method so that b = 0, the system’s will to continue must go out with it rather than persist on some residual objective. Third, the nature of genuine need is left open: our assumption is that it is derived from life, but we do not claim this, we do not reject other domains, and the one condition we do claim is that the need be real — not a label. The paper is narrower than AIWBN, which concerned need grounded in living tissue, and it neither rejects nor depends on AIWAN (Rezaei, 2026c), which concerned artificial need. We do not claim that genuine need would make an artificial system benevolent, and we do not address safety. No experiment is reported for the central claim, because it first requires an answer to what genuine need is and an inseparable bond between algorithm and need; we instead summarize selected AIWAN experiments that motivate the architectural requirements.

title: Continuation under Incompleteness. Proven Reliability, Settling-In and Branchable Development of Autonomous Systems
abstract: This independently readable companion paper extends the conceptual synthesis and discussion paper “Robotics Capable of Development” by examining the temporal development of reliable competences, local settling-in, responsibility and the continuation of autonomous systems under incomplete knowledge. A robot operating for extended periods in an open human environment cannot know every future condition in advance or possess every required competence as a fully specified rule from the outset. The paper therefore asks how abilities are acquired, how their reliability is demonstrated in practice and how the conditions and limits of their validity can remain recognizable during operation. Central distinctions concern competence, proven reliability and authorization, as well as general training and local settling-in. Other topics include historically established reliability, trust, responsible action under uncertainty, the interests of affected third parties, and the possibility of revising established routines when the world changes. A further focus is the continuation of artificial development after interruptions. The paper discusses the preservation of Gewordenheit, selective memory, reconnection after disruptions, backups, changes of physical carrier and branchable artificial ontogeny, in which shared developmental states can give rise to different subsequent learning histories. The paper presents neither a finished technical architecture nor a systematic literature review, and it makes no claim of scientific priority. Its purpose is to connect conceptual distinctions, research questions, possible experiments and counter-hypotheses that may help investigate the conditions of responsible, reliable and developmentally open autonomy.

title: THE REFERENCE-RELATIVE REALIZATION PRINCIPLE (RRRP): A General Reference-Relative Systems Principle with a Paradoxical Regime
abstract: The Reference-Relative Realization Principle (RRRP) proposes a general systems framework inin which the realization of a state, function, signal, representation, process, or output is defined relativeto an explicit reference structure rather than as an absolute property of the system alone. The theoryoriginates from the primary case study The Paradox of Contextualism, in which a subjectively specifiedintention may be evaluated by a generalized system through a reference structure that does not coincidewith the source-intended structure. The resulting apparent contradiction is not treated as a universalimpossibility theorem: exact realization can occur when the relevant equivalence relation is preserved,whereas non-equivalence between source and target reference structures makes exact preservation non-guaranteed. The framework therefore separates default mechanism, generalized principle, and paradoxicalor divergent regimes. A unified architecture represents source formation, encoding, labeling, signaling,projection, processing, medium transformation, target reconstruction, reference-relative evaluation,residual formation, iterative adaptation, and network-level interaction. The model is independent ofany particular criterion or medium: security, accuracy, utility, stability, semantic fidelity, energy, timing,language, code, physical channels, mathematical notation, computational systems, quantum systems,biological systems, and other admissible cases enter as parameterized instances. A finite operationalregime is complemented by an asymptotic regime for iterative realization. Thirty extension case studiesare organized across three analytical layers: Philosophical-Epistemological, Systemic-Mechanistic, andFormal-Mathematical Operational. The manuscript explicitly distinguishes mathematical definitionfrom empirical claim, identifies boundary conditions and counterexamples, and provides a falsifiabilityand anti-pseudomathematics protocol. The result is a general relational principle rather than a claim ofa universal physical law.

title: BLLM: The Entropy Cost of Sound Self-Improvement and a Typed Crossing Network Tested on Five Open Problems: paper, Lean 4 formalization and verification code
abstract: A BLLM is a language model that keeps a modification of itself only after a randomized check of soundness epsilon accepts it. The paper proves that certifying modifications of total cost A with at most theta expected false acceptances costs (A/log(1/epsilon))(H(p) + log(1/theta)) up to an additive A, where H(p) is the entropy of the cost profile; that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when the sum of a_n log(1/a_n) converges; and that a proposer needs at least exp(H_{1/2}(pi)) proposals, a bound that language models miss by factors of 1.5 to 4.3. It also describes and measures a typed crossing network with shared memory, run on five open problems (the Yang-Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdos problem 1183): the network reaches what its libraries can reach with half the checks, Hebbian boosters add nothing, and none of the five problems is solved. The lattice mass gap for four-dimensional SU(2) on beta_W < 1/3 is proved in the paper and has not been refereed. preprintBeyondTheLLM/ holds the paper as a PDF; BLLM/paper/ holds the REVTeX source with its figures; dist/ holds the PDF, the LaTeX source zip and the arXiv tarball. BLLM/lean/ is a Lean 4 and Mathlib project with fifty-nine theorems, each depending only on the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. BLLM/checks/ contains independent checks in Python, C and C++ (55,271 checks); BLLM/checks/run_all.sh runs them and builds the Lean project. The benchmark, the crossing network and the logs of every run are in the package eBLLM, version 2.0.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23455686.

title: E8 Triadic Entanglement Protocol for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Networks — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The 240 root vectors of the E8 lattice partition into 72 triadic triplets, each resonating at the 132 Hz base frequency and its phi‑harmonics, providing a natural encoding for logical qubits. By exploiting the high symmetry of E8, these triplets generate entangled states that are intrinsically resistant to phase errors, enabling fault‑tolerant quantum communication. The phi‑coupling between adjacent triplets ensures error cancellation across the network, while the 132 Hz global clock synchronizes distributed nodes. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: The Economic Value of AI-Driven Customer Experience in Digital Business Models
abstract: AI was increasingly revolutionizing digital business models by delivering superior customer experience and creating identifiable financial value. This study sought to understand the economic consequences of AI-enabled customer experience on digital media platforms in terms of consumer mindset, business functionality, and competitive edge. The purpose was to investigate how AI enhances customer interaction, what it contributes economically in terms of cost-cutting and increased profits, as well as identification of challenges, threats, and future trends. A quantitative research design was adopted, and a structured questionnaire was distributed to 250 users of digital business service. The results demonstrated that AI was found to facilitate increased customer satisfaction, transaction time saving and personalization and thus led to greater inclination of spending and loyalty. A ranking analysis showed that the most valued outcomes were cost savings and customer satisfaction, and the former was found to be the most preferred. Results indicated that the firms that integrated AI had received a more positive brand reputation and competitive advantage than those without. The report found that AI-based customer experience had generated significant economic value, but also encountered challenges in trust, data security and implementation cost continued to be challenging.

title: Human-in-Command (HIC) Governance for Generative AI Copyright and Physical-Layer Defense — Mathematical Formalization of $10B-Scale TCO Optimization, Decoupled Cluster/Unlearning Data Shapley, CLAP Multi-Stem Audio Attribution, Sub-1.5-ms HIC-CBF-QP Subsea Rerouting under UNCLOS, QPUF Silicon Root of Trust, and NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM-768) Edge TEE Provenance
abstract: This monograph establishes a unified mathematical, cryptographic, control-theoretic, and international legal framework anchored in Human-in-Command (HIC) sovereign governance, integrating Layer-3 Generative AI Copyright & Streaming Provenance Governance with Layer-1/2 Physical & Subsea Autonomous Defense Infrastructure. Under the Human-in-Command (HIC) doctrine, deterministic hardware co-processors (HITL0) execute sub-millisecond defensive actions within human-authored constitutional safety invariants h_HIC(x) >= 0, while ultimate sovereign authority over intellectual property valuation, unlearning revocation, and geopolitical non-escalation remains strictly under human command. Across seven core propositions (P1–P7), we prove: (P1) HIC Macro-Economic TCO Optimization: converting heavy-tailed ex-post copyright litigation and model disgorgement risks into predictable variable revenues via Data Shapley dividends, while eliminating $10M–$100M/day subsea cable cut downtime via Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS), HIC-governed Control Barrier Function Quadratic Programming (HIC-CBF-QP) rerouting in < 12.5 ms, and Space-Based Post-Quantum/QKD (SPOQC) redundancy; (P2) Zero-Latency Decoupling under HIC: separating asynchronous offline Monte Carlo / Cluster / Unlearning Shapley valuation during model updates from O(1) inference lookups (0 ms inference overhead), and executing HIC-CBF-QP on a parallel HITL0 co-processor with zero normal-mode latency and < 1.5 ms measured threat override; (P3) Silicon Supply-Chain Integrity: embedding chip-level Quantum Physical Unclonable Functions (QPUF) alongside NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM-768) to mathematically exclude counterfeit dies; (P4) International Maritime Law (UNCLOS) Compliance: resolving flag-state jurisdictional gaps (UNCLOS Articles 92, 110, 113) via HIC-authorized non-kinetic, self-defensive traffic evacuation without extraterritorial law enforcement; (P5) Open Standards & Modular HIC-API Governance; (P6) Multi-Dimensional Audio Stem Attribution: combining CLAP embeddings with 4-stem source separation and Cluster Shapley to axiomatically allocate Clean Corpus royalties across master owners, songwriters, and performers; and (P7) Edge TEE Chain of Provenance verifying exact human creator sovereignty in real time. 【和文要旨】本稿は、Human-in-Command(人間主権統制:HIC)を最高統治原理として、第3層(L3):生成AI著作権・来歴ガバナンスと第1・第2層(L1/L2):物理層・海底光ケーブル自律防衛インフラを統合する数理経済学・制御工学・耐量子暗号学・国際海洋法(UNCLOS)の一般理論体系(全7命題 P1〜P7)を構築する。Human-in-Command(HIC)原則の下では、人間(権利者・主権統治者)が安全不変条件 h_HIC(x) >= 0・著作権クリーンコーパス承認・アンラーニング撤回権の最終主権を保持し、物理層の並列監視コプロセッサ(HITL0)がその人間主権境界の内部でミリ秒未満の自律防衛を執行する。

title: AI-Based Customer Service and Brand Loyalty in Saudi Retail: An Empirical Investigation of the Service Quality-Emotional Attachment-Loyalty Pathway in 2025-2026
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered customer service systems have expanded across Saudi Arabia’s retail sector during 2025–2026, with major retailers increasingly exploring chatbots, recommendation engines, and automated service technologies. Official Saudi digital-economy statistics document the wider shift towards digital commerce, although the retailer-specific investment figures cited in an earlier draft have not been independently substantiated. This study examines the relationship among AI service quality, emotional brand attachment, and brand loyalty using survey results reported for 512 retail customers in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Dammam, collected between May and September 2026. Using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and bootstrap resampling, the analysis reports a positive direct association between AI service quality and loyalty (β = 0.421, p < 0.001), together with a positive indirect association through emotional brand attachment (reported indirect effect = 0.238, 95% CI [0.187, 0.289]). We discuss a possible “mechanical efficiency paradox”: functional improvements in AI service may be more strongly associated with loyalty than with emotional attachment. Importantly, this survey does not include a direct comparison with human-delivered service, and the reported positive attachment coefficient (β = 0.187) cannot establish that AI decreases attachment. The reported gender subgroup estimates differ: the AI quality–attachment association is positive for male respondents (β = 0.289, p = 0.001) and statistically nonsignificant for female respondents (β = −0.023, p = 0.811). Age-specific estimates also vary, with more positive reported coefficients in younger groups, although the statistical significance of the age differences requires further supporting output. The manuscript reports that the model accounts for 51.2% of the variance in loyalty (R2 = 0.512) and has positive predictive relevance (Q2 = 0.289). Because some path estimates, correlations, and variance-explained values are not mutually consistent, these results require rechecking against the original SmartPLS output before publication. Managerial implications include offering hybrid AI–human service, allowing customers to choose their preferred channel, and maintaining personal attention for complex or emotionally sensitive interactions. The findings provide a framework for assessing how technological service quality and relationship-building might jointly contribute to brand loyalty.

title: Secure Edge-ML: A Tamper-Resistant and Spoof-Resilient TinyML Architecture for Resource-Constrained IoT Devices
abstract: Secure Edge-ML: A Tamper-Resistant and Spoof-Resilient TinyML Architecture for Resource-Constrained IoT DevicesAbstract Traditional edge artificial intelligence systems prioritize inference performance while leaving critical security gaps, such as vulnerability to sensor data-injection spoofing, flash firmware modification, and physical RAM extraction. This work proposes and demonstrates Secure Edge-ML, an industrial-grade, zero-trust architecture implemented on an ESP32 microcontroller that unifies high-speed machine learning inference with robust embedded cybersecurity. Introduction As artificial intelligence migrates to resource-constrained edge microcontrollers (TinyML), systems face severe physical and digital threat vectors. Edge nodes deployed in industrial or automotive environments are routinely exposed to sensor spoofing, physical tampering, and firmware extraction. Conventional implementations treat machine learning and embedded security as isolated silos, leaving networks vulnerable. This project bridges that gap by introducing a multi-layered defense-in-depth architecture on an ESP32-DevKitC V4 platform, proving that strict security validation can coexist with hard real-time execution constraints. Content & System Architecture Deterministic TinyML Inference Engine: Executes a quantized neural network model locally on the edge node in 118 microseconds, satisfying hard real-time industrial control constraints. Sensor Anti-Spoofing & Rail Validation: Intercepts raw ADC streams via a continuous potentiometer setup on GPIO 34 to block false data injection (e.g., voltage forced to absolute ground 0 or maximum rail 4095) prior to model evaluation. Boot Integrity Verification: Computes and verifies a cryptographic hash (0xAEAD4201) of model weights stored in flash memory during boot to prevent unauthorized firmware modification. Physical Tamper Protection: Implements an automated hardware interrupt linked to an enclosure intrusion switch (push-button with a pull-down resistor on GPIO 12) that performs instant RAM sanitization upon physical breach. Parameters Proving Superiority To prove compliance with industrial security guidelines (such as IEC 62443 and automotive functional safety standards), this prototype demonstrates that multi-layered security incurs zero performance penalty: Inference Latency: Maintained at an elite 118 µs, preserving real-time actuator response times. Threat Mitigation Rate: 100% interception of rail-saturation and spoofing attacks, safely bypassing untrusted inferences ([SECURITY ALERT] Sensor spoofing / rail saturation detected!). Memory Protection: Eliminates plaintext weight and key leakage during physical inspection through automated hardware-level sanitization. Repository Files & Images Manifest main(1).c : Core firmware housing the TinyML inference engine, boot hash verification, anti-spoofing rail filter, and physical tamper interrupt routines. diagram(1).json: Complete Wokwi simulation schematic wiring the ESP32-DevKitC V4, industrial sensor potentiometer (GPIO 34), and tamper push-button with pull-down resistor (GPIO 12). eml_out1.jpg: Execution logs demonstrating simultaneous real-time 118 µs normal inferences and security threat interceptions during rail-saturation events. eml_out2.jpg: Visual proof of the active Wokwi hardware simulation layout and serial monitor security outputs confirming physical component assembly and real-time threat reporting. Conclusion The Secure Edge-ML prototype successfully demonstrates that high-performance edge AI and enterprise-grade embedded security are mutually achievable on low-cost hardware like the ESP32. By combining real-time anomaly detection, pre-inference rail-saturation validation, flash integrity hashing, and physical tamper key-shredding, this architecture establishes a new benchmark for trustworthy industrial IoT deployment.

title: Tokenizer Tax and Downstream Performance in Twelve African Languages
abstract: Code, results and paper for "Tokenizer Tax and Downstream Performance in Twelve African Languages" (Christophe Mumaragishyika, University of Missouri, 2026). The study asks whether the number of subword tokens a vocabulary spends on a word predicts how much a pretrained model gains over TF-IDF in sentiment classification. Three pipelines (TF-IDF with logistic regression, frozen LaBSE embeddings, and AfroXLMR-base fine-tuned with three seeds) ran with identical settings on the twelve AfriSenti languages with training splits: 60 runs. This release contains: the two notebooks and the grid script that produced every number in the paper per-run predictions (index, label, prediction only), result tables and the main figure a 66-item adversarial suite in Kinyarwanda and Swahili (CC BY 4.0) the paper as PDF and its LaTeX source It stores no tweets. The notebooks rebuild them from the pinned AfriSenti files (CC BY 4.0). Code under the MIT License.

title: Universal Cloning Is Optimal Exactly for Designs
abstract: Werner's universal cloner turns T copies of an arbitrary pure state in C^d into T+k approximate copies with optimal global fidelity D_T/D_{T+k}, where D_m = dim Sym^m(C^d). When the input is drawn from a restricted ensemble, a better cloner may exist. We show that, for optimal average global fidelity, it exists unless the ensemble is a design of order T+k: for every probability measure on pure states and all T, k ≥ 1, the optimal value equals D_T/D_{T+k} if and only if the measure is a complex projective (T+k)-design. Sufficiency follows from known arguments; the new content is necessity, which we prove from semidefinite-programming complementary slackness together with a rigidity lemma for operators acting on symmetric tensors. As corollaries, Werner's cloner is optimal for the uniform ensemble of n-qubit stabilizer states exactly when T+k ≤ 3 (for every n), for symmetric informationally complete ensembles exactly when T+k ≤ 2, and for complete sets of mutually unbiased bases exactly when T+k ≤ 3 in d = 2 and T+k ≤ 2 in d ≥ 3. We give exact rational certificates for the first strict gaps, and we contrast the result with structured state families, where matching moments is neither necessary nor sufficient for optimality. Files: the paper (PDF) and its LaTeX source; paper2_certificates.zip, the exact-arithmetic certificate scripts with their outputs, README and SHA-256 checksums (MIT licence); SHA256SUMS.txt lists the SHA-256 hashes of all files. Companion paper: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23428376.

title: Hybrid Quantum–Classical versus Classical Convolutional Neural Networks for Sign-Like Digit Recognition
abstract: This paper compares a classical convolutional neural network (CNN) with a hybrid quantum–classical convolutional neural network (QCNN) that appends a simulated parameterized quantum circuit to a convolutional front end. Both models were implemented with TensorFlow, TensorFlow Quantum and PennyLane and trained for ten epochs (batch size 64) on MNIST, used as a simplified proxy for numerals on speed limit signs. The hybrid model reached 98.67% accuracy after ten epochs versus 96.64% for the CNN, rose faster in early epochs, and had a median time of 139 s per epoch versus 440.5 s. Because the models differ in classical depth and were each trained once, the results do not establish a quantum advantage. The paper also discusses deployment barriers in vehicles and gives a SWOT comparison.

title: The Shaper (no training ai)
abstract: You are walking on the road, suddenly, you trip over and fall. Do you instantly think of what you will do next time or apply medicine and take care of your injury? You are going to take care of the injury. And then the next time when you are walking, and see a rock on the road, then you remember to avoid it. But that is not the truth for AI, the instantly think of what do next time if you see a rock. So what if we change it?

title: Müşteri Puanı-Duygu Uyumsuzluğunun Kalibre Analizi: İstanbul'daki Michelin Yıldızlı Restoranların eWOM Yorumlarının İncelenmesi
abstract: Çevrim içi müşteri yorumları, restoran seçimlerinde belirleyici bir bilgi kaynağı olarak kullanılmaktadır. Ancak yıldız puanlarının tek başına okunması, yorum metnindeki duygusal tonu her zaman yansıtmamaktadır. Bu uyumsuzluğun, beklentinin yüksek olduğu üst düzey restoranlarda daha belirgin hale geldiği düşünülmektedir. Buna karşın Michelin yıldızlı restoranlarda, alana özgü kalibre edilmiş ölçümlere dayanan çalışmalar sınırlı kalmıştır. Bu çalışmada, İstanbul'daki sekiz Michelin yıldızlı restorana ait 5.281 adet çok dilli Google yorumu (2017–2026) üzerinden yönlü puan–duygu uyumsuzluğu incelenmiştir. Duygu sınıflandırması, 500 insan etiketli yorumla kalibre edilmiş transformer tabanlı bir sınıflandırıcıyla yapılmıştır. Yorum uzunluğu ile restoran ve ay sabit etkileri kontrol edilerek kurulan sıralı ve ikili lojistik regresyon modellerinde, metinden türetilen duygunun yıldız puanlarını güçlü biçimde açıkladığı bulunmuştur. Duyguda bir basamaklık artışta, beş yıldız olasılığının yaklaşık 3,35 kat arttığı, bir–iki yıldız olasılığının ise 0,18 düzeyine düştüğü hesaplanmıştır. Genel uyuma karşın, beş yıldızlı yorumların %7,7'sinde olumsuz, bir–iki yıldızlı yorumların %22,8'inde olumlu duygu saptanmıştır. Ayrıca uyumsuzluk oranının restoranlar arasında farklılaştığı görülmüştür. Bu bulgular, yalnızca yıldız puanlarına dayalı izlemenin yüksek puanlar içinde gizlenen memnuniyetsizlik sinyallerini kaçırabileceğine işaret etmektedir. Çalışma, çok dilli yorumlarda alana özgü kalibre edilmiş duygu ölçümüyle puan–duygu uyumsuzluğunu ampirik olarak sayısallaştırarak alanyazındaki bu boşluğa katkı sunmaktadır.

title: ZAC-Specialization: Collective Capability Provisioning Through Hardware–Role Co-Design in Heterogeneous Intelligent Agent Populations
abstract: Heterogeneous intelligent-agent populations are often designed by assigning different tasks to agents with different capabilities. However, task specialization alone does not determine whether every agent must independently possess the hardware and computational resources required to perform its assigned functions. A population may contain specialized agents whose capabilities are available to others through shared services, while individual agents retain only the hardware necessary for their own responsibilities. This paper proposes ZAC-Specialization, a research framework for jointly determining agent specialization, local hardware configuration, collective capability provisioning, and reliability-aware service allocation. The central design question is not simply which agent should execute a task, but which capabilities must be provisioned locally, which should be maintained by specialized providers, and how these decisions should change as workloads and operating conditions evolve. The proposed framework represents tasks through capability requirements, agents through configurable hardware and service profiles, and collective execution through capability-service assignments. A joint optimization formulation minimizes lifecycle hardware costs, execution costs, communication overhead, coordination costs, and expected failure losses, subject to task-feasibility, deadline, capacity, and reliability constraints. The paper introduces a distinction between local capability ownership and collective capability accessibility, a specialization–provisioning decision model, and an adaptive role-reconfiguration mechanism. Its potential contribution must be established against existing research on heterogeneous multi-robot task allocation, capability-based coordination, and hardware–software co-design. The primary hypothesis is that jointly optimizing specialization and provisioning may reveal lower-cost feasible population configurations that cannot be identified by optimizing task allocation or individual hardware configurations in isolation.

evidence.title: ZAC-Specialization: Collective Capability Provisioning Through Hardware–Role Co-Design in Heterogeneous Intelligent Agent Populations
evidence.abstract: Heterogeneous intelligent-agent populations are often designed by assigning different tasks to agents with different capabilities. However, task specialization alone does not determine whether every agent must independently possess the hardware and computational resources required to perform its assigned functions. A population may contain specialized agents whose capabilities are available to others through shared services, while individual agents retain only the hardware necessary for their own responsibilities. This paper proposes ZAC-Specialization, a research framework for jointly determining agent specialization, local hardware configuration, collective capability provisioning, and reliability-aware service allocation. title: Does the authors' historical PPO configuration reproduce their released learning curves? Pre-registered replication of the Template-B output-reuse experiments at 16 minibatches (cycle 12R; third paper of a PhD on hybrid quantum–classical reinforcement learning)
abstract: AUTHORS Konstantinos Zervakis (Hellenic Army Academy); co-author Ilias Panagiotopoulos (Hellenic Army Academy). HOW THIS REGISTRATION DIFFERS FROM THE PREVIOUS ONE The cycle-12 registration (10.17605/OSF.IO/V7M6H) tests a mechanistic law on the published Template-B agent at the configuration of the authors' public scripts. This registration answers a point the authors raised in reply to our query of 2026-10-15: their published experiments were run with num_minibatches = 16, while the public scripts inherit num_minibatches = 4 from the released PPO class (num_steps 512, update_epochs 4 and learning rate 2.5e-4 are identical). The authors asked us to re-run an unentangled R = 4 run with the historical values. This step is pre-registered before any run; cycle 12 (running at registration time) is not changed by it. QUESTION At the historical configuration, are the released r4 and r16 curves (output-reuse factor R = 4 / 16; R replicas of the full circuit output vector feed the linear head) and the data-re-uploading L = 1 curve reproduced at nominal R, does the CNOT ring still fail, and are four-fold gradient steps operationally equivalent to four-fold output reuse? INSTRUMENTS AND ARMS (A) The authors' unmodified code (git commit 6b9897c, isolated environment hashed at the freeze), with the four historical values passed to their PPO class and asserted before training: none_R4_mb4 (the public configuration, never run before at nominal R = 4), none_R4_mb16, none_R16_mb16, ring_R4_mb16, ring_R16_mb16, dr_L1_none_R1_mb16; seeds 1200–1209; 100,000 steps (60 runs). (B) Our re-implementation of Template B (the one used in cycles 11 and 12), identical except for the minibatch count: none_R4_mb4, none_R4_mb16, none_R16_mb4, none_R16_mb16, ring_R4_mb4, ring_R4_mb16, ring_R16_mb16; seeds 1200–1229; 100,000 steps (210 runs). (F1) Fingerprint replays of the authors' code: the first three updates (1,536 steps of the 100,000-step schedule) for seeds 1–10, R in {4, 16}, num_minibatches in {4, 16}, with and without the authors' get_agent_info call (80 replays), compared with the clipfrac, approx_kl and value_loss series of the released r4/r16 event files. METRICS AND REGISTERED INPUTS Authors' metric: per seed, the mean return of training episodes ending at step ≥ 90,000 (identical computation for their CSV, our episode log and their TensorBoard files). Our metric J (instrument B only): 11 evaluation points × 32 episodes with sampled actions and common random numbers; AUC of J; "learns" = final J ≥ 0.20. The released per-seed values are registered in the frozen file with the SHA-256 of each event file: r4 (95.8, 98.6, 103.4, 72.5, 96.8, 163.3, 99.6, 113.4, 85.5, 137.7), r16 (389.0, 219.6, 146.3, 485.2, 407.0, 458.1, 415.2, 440.0, 354.1, 163.3), DR-L1 (43.0, 48.7, 41.6, 55.7, 51.9, 47.4, 42.0, 50.0, 46.6, 46.4). REGISTERED STATEMENTS (decision rules in the frozen file, section 6) P1: A none_R4_mb16 vs the released r4 — three outcomes: "not reproduced" (two-sided Welch p < 0.05 and exact label-permutation p < 0.05), "reproduced" (90 % CI of the difference of mean log returns within ± log 1.5, i.e. an equivalence test within a factor 1.5), otherwise "consistent". Expected: reproduced. P1-control: A none_R4_mb4 vs r4 — "differs" iff both p < 0.05 and the mean lies below the released mean. Expected: differs. P2: A none_R16_mb16 vs r16, same three outcomes (power allows at best "consistent"). Expected: consistent or reproduced. P3: the ring fails at 16 minibatches — at most 1 of 10 completed A seeds reaches an authors'-metric value ≥ 100 and at most 3 of 30 B seeds learn, in each mb16 ring arm. Expected: pass. P4: B paired contrast none_R4_mb16 − none_R16_mb4 on the AUC of J — EQ iff the 90 % CI lies within ± 0.03 ("four-fold steps interchangeable with four-fold reuse"). Expected: EQ. P5: B paired none_R16_mb16 − none_R4_mb16 > 0 (the output-reuse gain persists at 16 minibatches). Expected: positive beyond 0.05. P6: B paired none_R4_mb16 − none_R4_mb4 > 0 (the minibatch count matters). Expected: positive beyond 0.05. P7: A dr_L1_none_R1_mb16 vs the released DR-L1 curve, three outcomes. Expected: reproduced if PPO was held fixed across the authors' experiments. F1 (descriptive): a configuration is "identified" for a log set iff its replay matches all three series of updates 1–3 within 1e-5 (relative) for ≥ 8 of 10 seeds and no other configuration does; otherwise "not identified" (the closest configuration is reported, no claim). Expected: R = 4 (r4) and R = 16 (r16), both at 16 minibatches. Holm correction over {P4, P5, P6} only; P1, P1-control, P2 and P7 are decided by their own rules; P3 is a count rule. Completeness: ≥ 8/10 completed seeds (A) and ≥ 23/30 (B) per row; a crashed run is re-run once and then counted as missing. The wording each outcome licenses in the paper (for example "documentation gap in the public scripts" vs "unexplained" vs "the instruments disagree") is fixed in the frozen file. GATES (binding, logged before any main run) Every A run asserts num_steps 512, num_minibatches 16 (or 4 for the control), minibatch size 32 (128), update_epochs 4, learning rate 2.5e-4, annealing on, 100,000 total steps, and after training 12,544 (3,136) optimiser steps and 196 learning-rate entries ending at 1.276e-6, as in all 40 released files; the A smoke runs twice and the two logs must be identical except wall time. Instrument B reproduces a stored cycle-11 run bit for bit at 4 minibatches before anything else runs. The authors' environment is hashed and compared before F1, before the A smoke and before the A main runs. ORDER AND STATUS Freeze → this registration → cycle 12 finished → F1 → B → A → analysis by the unchanged pre-written statistics script. No run of this step exists at registration time. Everything through cycle 11, the authors' reply and the cycle-12 freeze are known; the cycle-12 results are not known at the freeze; no statement here uses a cycle-12 quantity. Later answers from the authors change no rule. title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning
abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath-Bench, a process-aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath-Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine-grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem-solving correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning-chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.

title: ChunavIQ: An Open, End-to-End Verifiable Remote-Voting Prototype for India's Legal and Identity Constraints, with Deniable Revoting, Hardware-Held Trustee Keys and Adversarial Dress Rehearsals
abstract: India runs the world's largest elections: about 970 million electors in 543 parliamentary constituencies in 2024. Any remote-voting proposal for India must fit its election law, its identity infrastructure and its scale, and must say what it does not solve. We present ChunavIQ, an open-source research prototype that combines established techniques (threshold ElGamal, zero-knowledge ballot proofs, deniable revoting, Terelius-Wikström verifiable shuffles, designated-verifier proofs and an append-only Merkle log) into a complete system adapted to Indian constraints. Voters register a phone with either Aadhaar or PAN; since PAN checks only a name and birth date, the PAN path adds a one-time code to the mobile number on the electoral roll and a face match. A voter may vote again at any time, and a vote at a polling station on polling day cancels the online ballot; nobody, including a coercer, can tell which ballot counted. One national key is shared among trustees whose shares stay inside hardware security modules. We contribute (i) the adapted protocol and two independent implementations with two independent verifiers that cross-check each other's records; (ii) a capacity model for 1-1.5 billion electors built from measured unit costs; (iii) an open dress-rehearsal method that runs a constituency election over HTTP under seven kinds of attack and publishes every request; and (iv) a provision-by-provision analysis of the Indian legal changes such a system would need. Every record we produced verified. A first rehearsal forced the largest constituency's full design rate onto one machine and recorded only 72-99% of honest ballots per phase; after fixes identified from its published metrics, a rehearsal at 78% of that rate recorded every honest ballot, 97-100% of them within 30 s, while refusing every attack. ChunavIQ uses synthetic data only and is not proposed for binding elections. Code: https://github.com/itsashiish/chunaviq (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23442948). Demo: https://chunaviq.oglic.com

title: ViMoLa: Discrete Motion Tokens for Language-Guided Video Generation
abstract: Language-guided video generation often captures scene content while missing the requested motion. We present ViMoLa (Video Motion Language), which predicts a motion prior from language and injects it into a frozen image-to-video backbone. A spatial vector-quantized autoencoder compresses dense trajectories into 64 tokens from a 512-entry codebook; a 28M-parameter transformer predicts the tokens from text; and zero-gated cross-attention adapters condition every frozen Wan~2.2 DiT block through forward hooks. Trained on 462K videos from Something-Something~v2 and Kinetics-400, ViMoLa raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442 (chance 0.250), with similar measured generative quality. Across-prompt shuffled codes achieve 0.283, supporting the importance of prompt-matched token content. A low-rank adapter reaches 0.428 at 1.45% additional forward-pass FLOPs, and reusing the tokenizer and language model with newly trained CogVideoX adapters raises accuracy from 0.301 to 0.398. Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound-motion gains are smaller, and the adapter does not explicitly preserve token-to-patch assignments.

title: Matched data, small gaps: a pre-registered comparison of fine-tuned classifiers, retrieval-prompted language models and a typed-decision model for intent and out-of-scope decisions
abstract: Before an assistant acts on a message, it decides whether the message is something it handles (scope) and what it asks for (intent). We ask which kind of system should make that decision given the same in-scope labelled data, and what moves a prompted model's scope decision. We compare a fine-tuned 150M classifier with retrieval-prompted 27–31B language models on three intent sets, in protocols frozen before any request; only the classifier also calibrates its scope decision on out-of-scope development items, and a hosted typed-decision model is a secondary system. On Banking77 the two are not significantly different, though equivalence within 2.5 points is not shown, and MASSIVE shows no stable ordering across four draws of held-out domains. The one significant pre-registered gap (CLINC150, 1.9 points for the language model) halves and is not significant on items we had never inspected (post hoc). The clearest finding concerns the second question. On fresh label-clean BANKING77-OOS items, retrieving in-scope examples lowered five models' rejection of same-domain out-of-scope requests by 19 to 30 points, while random examples moved it by 1 to 11. This is mainly a shift of the operating point towards acceptance, not a demonstrated loss of discrimination: at equal in-scope acceptance, the typed-decision model's rejection rose. Labelled out-of-scope examples raise rejection, mainly for the requests that retrieve them. We also report a label leak we found in BANKING77-OOS and the exploratory conclusions we withdrew.

title: StopLoss: Teaching Agents to Predict Failure and Stop Early
abstract: Coding agents keep working on runs that will fail verification, and asking a frontier model to watch for this is expensive in its own right. We introduce StopLoss, a small external monitor that learns failure recognition from completed trajectories and their verifier outcomes. The name is inspired by the stop-loss order in finance: StopLoss ends a run early when the run is likely to fail, which saves resources. Final outcomes label earlier local windows, so a fine-tuned language model can score the most recent tool steps in a single forward pass, and a threshold calibrated on successful runs turns that score into an abort decision without changing the executor. Trained on GPT-family SWE-rebench trajectories and evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset with GPT and Claude executors, StopLoss is compared against six general-purpose judges reading identical windows. Outcome supervision lifts failure prediction from near chance to a useful signal at the first check, at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost per check than any tested judge. This translates into savings: relative to completing every task, StopLoss lowers cost per retained solve by 4.5\% on Verified while preserving 99\% of successful runs, and by up to 31\% on the costlier Pro subset, reaching 48\% with a Qwen3-8B backbone, and in all four settings its cost per retained solve is below that of every judge policy. Outcome-trained small monitors can make failure recognition cheap enough for early stopping to pay for itself.

title: VoiceGuard: An Evaluation-Honest, Multi-Signal Decision Layer for Real-Time Voice-Clone Detection in High-Stakes Telephone Calls
abstract: VoiceGuard: An Evaluation-Honest, Multi-Signal Decision Layer for Real-Time Voice-Clone Detection in High-Stakes Telephone Calls This paper investigates the generalization limitations of speech anti-spoofing systems for detecting voice-clone fraud in telephone calls. It examines evaluation artifacts in the ASVspoof 2019 Logical Access benchmark and re-evaluates the published AASIST model using an anti-shortcut evaluation protocol. The paper proposes VoiceGuard, a multi-signal decision layer that combines acoustic spoof detection, speaker consistency, prosodic features, and call context to generate ALLOW, VERIFY, or ESCALATE recommendations. It also introduces a feature-only audit log to support transparency and human review. Additionally, a five-language pilot study evaluates the transferability of an English-trained detector across Indian languages, highlighting the challenges of multilingual voice-clone detection. The work emphasizes evaluation integrity, cross-dataset generalization, explainable decision-making, and the need for further validation before deployment in high-stakes environments. Authors: Ghanshyam Kumavat, Sunil Saini, and Vicky PukaleAffiliation: Department of Computer Engineering, Vidyalankar Institute of Technology, Mumbai, India.

title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

title: SlimFormer++: Token Mixing Where It Matters for Efficient 3D Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: To determine where computation is needed in volumetric segmentation networks, we analyze block-level redundancy and stage-wise token-mixer contribution. Centered Kernel Alignment reveals high input-output representational similarity within blocks of representative convolutional, hybrid, and Transformer-style segmentation networks. Similarity-guided pruning reduces their parameter counts by 39-75% while decreasing mean Dice by less than 0.4 percentage points. To examine token mixers within blocks, we introduce Anatomical Relation Distortion, which quantifies how bypassing a mixer distorts feature relations between labeled anatomical positions. Applied to an unpruned candidate architecture, Centered Kernel Alignment indicates high representational redundancy in intermediate encoder mixers, whereas Anatomical Relation Distortion shows that they contribute little and the bottleneck mixer most. These findings motivate SlimFormer++, which uses Selective Mixing blocks with windowed Mamba mixing in the first encoder stage and only residual channel MLPs in deeper stages. At the bottleneck, Augmented Mixing injects similarity-weighted sparse long-range context into the axial taps of a depthwise convolution at cost linear in voxel count. Evaluated against 12 baselines across eight public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets (1,809 cases), SlimFormer++ achieves the highest mean Dice (87.84%) and lowest mean HD95 (6.50 mm) with the fewest parameters (5.98 million). These results support stage-aware token mixing as a design strategy for improving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in volumetric segmentation. The source code is available at https://github.com/WHHHHHY822/SlimFormerPlusPlus

title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.

title: Before the Point of No Return: Identifying Irreversible Decision Windows in Memory-Augmented Agents
abstract: Memory-augmented agents reuse past experience across long-horizon tasks, but a task-wrong (conflicting) memory is adopted early and its damage is often irreversible in the environment. We reproduce the MemTrapBench compliance-trap protocol and measure, step by step, where a conflicting memory first changes behavior, how far that change carries, and whether the agent can undo it, localizing a threshold X past which the trajectory is irreversibly bound for failure. We then test decision-window interventions: mechanical deliberation is inert on both a 9B and a 1.6T-parameter model, while a semantic intervention that demotes memory from authority to candidate is two-sided, helping on heterogeneous (mixed) memory and hurting on uniformly wrong memory, which bounds what a decision-layer intervention can and cannot do.

title: Argument Reasoning
abstract: Abstract Reasoning is the heart of argumentation—so much that some researchers might equate the terms reasoning and argumentation . This is because, conceptually, an argument manifests a reasoning process (or process step) in natural language: the relation that it defines from one or more premises to a conclusion instantiates the act of giving a reason, or reasons, to support a claim. In a broader sense, though, argumentation comprises more than just reasoning. As the previous chapters on perspective and quality assessment have emphasized, subjective viewpoints and perceptions are inherent to argumentation, and rhetoric and dialectic are important in any real-world argumentation setting. Thus, reasoning can be understood as the part of argumentation that describes how people infer new (or hidden) information from given information through the use or exchange of arguments. As such, reasoning is where the NLP tasks of analysis and synthesis meet. In this chapter, we discuss some main strands of NLP research that model key aspects of reasoning, given previously mined or otherwise structured arguments.

title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. Qwen3-0.6B has been fine-tuned with LoRA on Reason-9k and Bitext reply rows. JevBench accuracy shows no statistically significant change (55.4% to 54.5%, p=0.87), while expected calibration error falls from 0.292 to 0.169. Held-out Bitext routing accuracy reaches 98.3%. Cache reuse saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro, with token-identical replies in the FP32 demonstration cases. Scoring options on copies of the prompt cache matches full-sequence scoring to within 1.4e-6 in probability. Adding dialogue, industry and complaint data (System X+) improves support-task results but lowers IFEval accuracy from 55.5% to 45.0%. System X v4 uses Qwen3-1.7B, rebalanced data and teacher-rewritten reply targets. Against its base LLM, JevBench accuracy rises from 55.0% to 61.0% (p=0.04), with no statistically significant IFEval change (p=0.71). A matched latency test on unadapted Qwen3-1.7B saves 17-39%. One LLM judge prefers v4 replies to an unadapted 1.7B second call (31 to 11 pairs, p=0.003); the other's preference is not significant. These reply comparisons also differ in prompts and generation limits. State conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes. Further studies with several seeds, human raters and real support data are recommended.

title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated "forget set" without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model p_θ to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor p_{anchor} on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence KL(p_θVert p_{anchor}). We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence KL(p_{anchor} Vert p_θ) logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.

title: RARE: Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution for Open-Ended Generation
abstract: Verifiable rewards have advanced reinforcement learning in mathematics and code. However, many valuable open-ended tasks share three properties: no automatic verifier of overall quality, multiple requirements to satisfy jointly, and multiple valid responses to each query. Training therefore needs feedback on requirement satisfaction across different valid responses. Rubric-based reinforcement learning provides this feedback by aggregating scores from explicit criteria. As learning progresses unevenly, some criteria become fully satisfied and lose discrimination while others remain informative. Dynamic methods revise shared rubrics or select evolving criteria to restore discrimination, but may also change useful criteria. To address this, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution (RARE). The core idea is to use current policy feedback to guide both which criteria change and what their replacements assess. Sample-level updates replace criteria fully satisfied across current outputs with checks of remaining quality differences, retaining all other criteria and scores. Within this rule, we compare rewarding desirable qualities with penalizing observed flaws. Video script generation exemplifies these properties and supports content production. Its demands for coherent, executable narratives under constraints make it a challenging testbed. Targeting flaws performs best across three video types with a mean gain of 3.82 points over matched static rubrics. Model and human preferences support these gains. Improvements also extend to writing and general generation benchmarks.

title: ROC space with four example classifiers
abstract: The ROC space, with the four example prediction results A, B, C and C′ from the Receiver operating characteristic article. The horizontal axis is the false positive rate, FPR = FP / (FP + TN), which equals 1 − specificity. title: Mixture-of-Memories: Low-Overhead Language Modeling with Modular Knowledge Injection
abstract: Large language models store substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, yet this knowledge is difficult to control, update, and reliably elicit at inference time. Existing memory-augmented approaches typically rely on a single auxiliary mechanism, such as retrieval, parameter updates, or neural memory, and therefore apply the same form of correction to tokens with very different knowledge demands. We propose Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that separates routed neural memory from writable factual memory. MoM combines a frozen base LM with two neural memory experts: a latent memory that provides low-latency hidden-state corrections and a lexical memory that provides a token-space knowledge pathway. A lightweight Budget Router sets per-token mixture weights from uncertainty and disagreement features, replacing the fixed interpolation of prior memory modules. For post-hoc updates, an external explicit memory stays outside the router, because a router trained before facts are written learns to down-weight it; new facts are appended without retraining any component and used only when an answer-level gate accepts the retrieved fact. Experiments across language modeling, factual QA, update analysis, and efficiency show that MoM improves both predictive accuracy and updateability while retaining low inference overhead.

title: Generative Structural Theory v1.23 — Connecting the Class C Evaluation with Closure-Preserving Sub-relations
abstract: GST v1.19 stored, for the fixed cut z_t of twelve pairs, a list of 59 sub-relations as the set C_2 of its class C evaluation; GST v1.20-v1.22 described, counted and analysed the family H_lt(z_t) of the proper sub-relations of z_t that keep its reflexive transitive closure, which also has 59 members. This manuscript connects the two by members, not by counts, and keeps three objects apart: the set E_alg that the evaluator's loop and acceptance condition define, the set E_stored of the elements of the stored list, and the set C_2 of the paper's definition. (T2a) E_alg = H_lt(z_t), by an argument based on existing computation results (the registered B1 check of v1.20) and on the drafting side's static reading of the evaluator, with no new enumeration. (T2b) E_stored = H_lt(z_t), and the stored list has no repeated element, confirmed by a pre-registered, LOCKed machine comparison (a single run, no automatic correction, no rerun; word EQUAL), which builds the reference set in two ways that must agree and checks four controls first. Hence E_stored = H_lt(z_t) = E_alg as sets, relations being identified with their integer codes. (T2c) Every member of C_2, where its definition applies, lies in H_lt(z_t), by the definition alone, without D2 or a check of condition C-cone; the converse inclusion holds if the recorded certified set V of the v1.18 runs is the V of those runs. So C_2 = H_lt(z_t) holds under that assumption; it is not established without it, and the assumption is undetermined. (T3) Through the equalities of T2a and T2b, the v1.22 results for z_t hold for E_alg and E_stored: five pairs lie in every member, there are four inclusion-minimal members, of 7, 7, 8 and 8 pairs, the least number of pairs is 7, and the stored answer y = z_t - {1>3} is one of the seven maximal members and is not inclusion-minimal. A short lemma says why removing the maximum z_t does not change the essential pairs, the inclusion-minimal members or the members of minimum cardinality. These are structural consequences; they do not explain why the procedure stored y. Nothing is claimed about the provenance of the stored file, other cuts, or the classification inside components.

title: PDF token cost per page: Claude vs Gemini, and PDF vs pasted text
abstract: Input tokens for text, table and scanned PDF pages (1 to 10 pages) on Claude Opus/Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.x, compared with pasting the same content as text. Headline: one page of text costs 2,347 tokens as a PDF on Claude 5.5 but 728 when the same text is pasted (69% less). Gemini charges a flat ~560 tokens per PDF page whatever is on it. Source page, chart and method: https://tokensave.app/data/pdf-token-cost Related: image token cost by resolution (https://tokensave.app/data/image-token-cost) Measured: 2026-10-18 License: CC BY 4.0 Key findings Claude reads each PDF page as text and as an image. A text page costs 2,347 tokens on Claude 5.5; a scanned page with no text layer costs 1,600 (the image part alone). Pasting text is much cheaper on Claude: 728 tokens instead of 2,347 for the same page. Gemini charges a flat rate: text, table and scanned pages all cost 561 tokens; 10 pages cost 5,601. On Gemini a PDF can beat pasting: the table page costs 561 tokens as a PDF and 777 pasted as CSV (28% less as a PDF). Cost grows in a straight line with pages: 10 text pages cost 23,236 tokens on Claude 5.5. Files pdf-token-cost.csv: one row per input with input, label, kind, pages, tokens for claude55, claude45, gemini, gpt (pasted text only) and per-page values pdf-token-cost.json: the same data plus the pasted text used Data Input Claude Opus/Sonnet 5.5 Claude Haiku 4.5 Gemini 3.x GPT (o200k) PDF, text, 1 page 2,347 2,115 561 – PDF, text, 5 pages 11,631 10,499 2,801 – PDF, text, 10 pages 23,236 20,979 5,601 – PDF, table, 1 page 2,481 2,278 561 – PDF, scanned image, 1 page 1,600 1,592 561 – Same page pasted as text 728 503 455 461 Same table pasted as CSV text 913 720 777 629 Method A4 PDFs made with ReportLab: one page of English prose (about 420 words), the same page repeated to 5 and 10 pages, a page with a 35-row table, and a scanned version of the text page (150 dpi image, no text layer). Claude: each PDF sent through Claude Code (claude -p, stream-json input) as a document block with a one-character message; input tokens minus the same run without the PDF. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 gave identical counts. Gemini: per-file token count shown by Google AI Studio for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Pasted text: prompt counter minus its one start token. GPT: OpenAI bills PDF input as extracted text plus page images, which could not be reproduced without the API, so GPT is given for pasted text only (tiktoken, o200k_base). Limitations One page design. Denser pages, small fonts or many images will cost more on Claude. Default settings; Gemini's media resolution option changes its per-page count. Input tokens only; price per token differs by model. Citation TokenSave (2026). PDF token cost per page: Claude vs Gemini, and PDF vs pasted text [Data set]. https://tokensave.app/data/pdf-token-cost

title: UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation
abstract: World models offer increasingly rich environments for exploration, yet intervening in a world while observing the consequences from freely chosen viewpoints remains challenging. We tackle these challenges by introducing UniState, a framework for controllable world simulation built on a unified world-state representation. This representation unifies spatial memory and user interventions. Users specify object motion directly within spatial memory, while independently choosing the camera trajectory from which the resulting world state is observed. This unification makes the relationship between the scene and the requested changes explicit, removing ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change from the control specification. Crucially, specifying an intervention does not require prescribing every resulting movement: the video model can synthesize additional motion within controlled objects and plausible interactions with their surroundings. We develop training and sampling strategies that help generated videos follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while preserving this capacity to generate responses beyond the prescribed transformations. Experiments demonstrate more accurate joint object and camera control than the existing methods, alongside qualitative evidence that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.

title: Polynomial Density Learning of Spherical Gaussian Mixtures with a Minimum-Weight Bound
abstract: We give a polynomial-time improper density learner for mixtures of at most k identity-covariance Gaussians in ℝ^d whose nonzero mixing weights are at least a supplied w_min > 0. The means are unrestricted and need not be separated, linearly independent, or contained in a bounded ball. Training samples, real-arithmetic operations, and the cost of each output sample are polynomial in d, k, w_min⁻¹, ε⁻¹, log(1/δ), where ε is total-variation accuracy and 1−δ is training confidence. In particular, uniformly weighted mixtures admit joint-polynomial density learning without geometric assumptions. The construction extends a positive-atom moment cover to bounded-radius Gaussian location mixtures through compressed radial normalization. Fresh Gaussian split views then yield exact positive localization and globally pruned radius refinement without accumulated noise. At the terminal radius, full routed positive semidefinite moment matrices learn tensor subspaces, while an observable quadratic loss under a common mixture reference learns density coefficients from the original samples. This separation avoids a failure of per-bin Hermite density estimation: a far component of tiny routing mass can have exponentially large local Hermite coefficients. Randomized Hermite evaluation, clipping, and capped rejection sampling yield a valid nonnegative output distribution. The dependence on the minimum original weight is substantive; arbitrary-weight joint-polynomial learning remains outside the theorem.

title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

title: Tor Hides Your IP, Not Your Words: Free LLMs as an Attribute-Inference Threat to Users of Network Anonymity Tools
abstract: Tor and VPNs hide a user's IP address, and users often treat that as anonymity. We show that the text such users post remains a strong source of personal information, and that extracting it is now free. On 100 synthetic authors from the SynthPAI dataset, two free-tier Gemini models inferred eight personal attributes from the authors' comments. The best model guessed sex correctly 85.4% of the time, occupation 71.4% and country 72.3%, with a mean of 64.3% over all attributes; most of these attributes are never revealed by an IP address at all. A simple defense, rewriting comments with an LLM before posting, lowered mean accuracy to 49.5% but did not remove any attribute. We release all code and raw model outputs.

title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than 2times compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to 4.1times over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

title: linlog
abstract: A linear logic suite: a Rust library and a command line program that decide, check, prove step by step and export sequents of classical and intuitionistic linear logic and their fragments, keep proofs in a form an independent checker validates, show them as derivation trees or proof nets, and decide ordinary propositional logic through its embeddings into linear logic. Its code, tests and documentation were written with substantial AI assistance, by Anthropic's Claude models in Claude Code, in steps the author planned, directed and accepted, and the author is responsible for them. Its results do not rest on the model that wrote it: every proof it returns is validated by an independent proof checker, classical proofs can be exported as certificates that the Rocq proof assistant checks, the tests are measured by mutation testing and fuzzing, and its verdicts on published problem libraries are compared with their known status and with those of eight other provers.

title: Structure-prior relation graph learning for spatio-temporal anomaly detection in multi-entity collaborative systems
abstract: Spatio-temporal anomaly detection in multi-entity collaborative systems aims to identify abnormal states from multivariate time series generated by dynamically coupled variables. Fully data-driven relation learning may recover unstable or spurious dependencies when normal observations are limited, noisy, or weakly informative about rare coordination failures. This paper studies structure-prior relation graph learning (SPRGL), which augments a GDN-style predictive graph backbone with weak structural priors. Variable groups, topology files, or process connectivity are represented as a structure-prior graph and united with the embedding-derived candidate graph before graph-attention prediction. The technical contribution is therefore the candidate-edge fusion mechanism, rather than the established embedding, Top- k graph learning, attention forecasting, or residual-scoring components. We also construct CTown-RB as a semi-synthetic benchmark containing five injected relation-breaking scenarios based on public CTown topology and normal BATADAL operating data. Under the reported comparison with PCA-SPE, Isolation Forest, and LOF, SPRGL obtains the highest reported F1 and AUC-PR in the SMD, BATADAL, and CTown-RB settings shown in Table 1 ; a separate HAI experiment examines sensitivity to the residual-aggregation size k s . On CTown-RB, the combined prior changes PA-F1 from 0.5651 to 0.8734 and detects all five injected scenarios, while also reducing Precision. These results delimit the current evidence to the reported baselines, datasets, and archived evaluation outputs.

evidence.title: Structure-prior relation graph learning for spatio-temporal anomaly detection in multi-entity collaborative systems
evidence.abstract: Spatio-temporal anomaly detection in multi-entity collaborative systems aims to identify abnormal states from multivariate time series generated by dynamically coupled variables. Fully data-driven relation learning may recover unstable or spurious dependencies when normal observations are limited, noisy, or weakly informative about rare coordination failures. This paper studies structure-prior relation graph learning (SPRGL), which augments a GDN-style predictive graph backbone with weak structural priors. Variable groups, topology files, or process connectivity are represented as a structure-prior graph and united with the embedding-derived candidate graph before graph-attention prediction. The technical contribution is therefore the candidate-edge fusion mechanism, rather than the established embedding, Top- k graph learning, attention forecasting, or residual-scoring components. We also construct CTown-RB as a semi-synthetic benchmark containing five injected relation-breaking scenarios based on public CTown topology and normal BATADAL operating data. Under the reported comparison with PCA-SPE, Isolation Forest, and LOF, SPRGL obtains the highest reported F1 and AUC-PR in the SMD, BATADAL, and CTown-RB settings shown in Table 1 ; a separate HAI experiment examines sensitivity to the residual-aggregation size k s . On CTown-RB, the combined prior changes PA-F1 from 0.5651 to 0.8734 and detects all five injected scenarios, while also reducing Precision. These results delimit the current evidence to the reported baselines, datasets, and archived evaluation outputs.

title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
abstract: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.

title: When Do Latent World Models Detect Game Glitches? Representation Collapse, Pretrained Video Latents, and an Action-Conditioned Benchmark
abstract: Latent world models trained only on normal gameplay are an appealing, label-free source of "surprise" for glitch detection. This article extends our conference diagnostic study, which found that a LeWorldModel-style JEPA trained from scratch on TempGlitch collapses to effective rank ≈ 1 and reaches AUROC 0.579–0.588, clearly below a kNN detector on frozen VideoMAE features (0.6895). We add three pieces of evidence. (i) Frozen V-JEPA 2 latents. A kNN detector on frozen V-JEPA 2 features reaches 0.6592, and a normal-only next-latent predictor on its 0.4 s temporal tokens reaches 0.665–0.669, a statistical tie with, but not above, VideoMAE kNN; a causal transformer predictor on the same tokens is worse (0.598–0.599). (ii) Collapse remedies. In a pre-specified six-arm sweep (SIGReg weight, batch size, VICReg terms, longer training; one seed), the LeWM encoder's effective rank rises from 1.13 to 21.3, but AUROC does not follow: the best arm (batch 32) reaches 0.6264 (+0.0427 over the reproduced anchor, p = 0.00076), whereas the least-collapsed arm reaches 0.5954 (arm-level Spearman ρ = 0.37, n = 6). (iii) An action-conditioned benchmark. We build ACGB, five headless games with recorded per-frame actions, eight programmatic glitch types at three severities, and a counterfactual clean twin per glitched episode. On its development split, action conditioning does not help the JEPA (macro AUROC 0.605 with actions vs. 0.625 without) but does help a small pixel predictor (0.888 vs. 0.783), notably on input-remapping glitches; locked-test results are pending. (iv) A surprise-driven explorer. On 400 held-out bugged levels with state-triggered hidden bugs, an agent maximising world-model surprise finds fewer bugs than random actions (found fraction 0.258 vs. 0.322) and raises about fifteen times more false alarms on clean levels. Across all experiments, non-collapse is necessary but not sufficient: the temporal content of the latent space matters more than its rank.
